records.title: Actions
records.summary: Every interaction carries an id a server can trust When a user presses a button on an agent-generated surface, the runtime asks your action policy first. Only an action the policy executed leaves the runtime, through onActionEnvelope . A de
records.text: Every interaction carries an id a server can trust When a user presses a button on an agent-generated surface, the runtime asks your action policy first. Only an action the policy executed leaves the runtime, through onActionEnvelope . A denied action never does. The envelope Put envelope.forwardedProps into the next AG-UI run input: Field Meaning --- --- userAction The A2UI action exactly as the renderer produced it. It is never modified actionId A globally unique UUIDv7 minted once per interaction. Two tabs, or one tab after a reload, never share one. A server uses it to make handling idempotent heldVersion The version the surface held when the action fired, so a server can tell a stale action from a current one. Absent for a surface with no versioned state dataModel Present only when the surface sets sendDataModel The runtime does not arbitrate duplicates. De-duplicating by actionId is the server's job, which is why the id is stable across retries. Two different ids A v1.0 wantResponse action can also carry an actionId . That is a correlation id, shaped surface:component:n , unique only within one runtime instance, that matches an actionResponse to its action. It is unchanged. The envelope's actionId is an idempotency id and is global. They do different jobs. Do not use one for the other. Retry retryAction resends the original envelope under the same id. The runtime owns retry because a host that resent on its own would mint a new id and defeat idempotency. The resent envelope keeps the heldVersion and data model from when the action fired. It returns false for an unknown id (the last 100 envelopes are retained) or when no handler is installed. Stale-action rejection A server that sees an action built on an old version can reject it and return what the client is missing. Pass that to applyStaleActionRejection : a2ui operations are the operations since the version the client held, and surfaceVersions are the versions they bring each surface to. They go through the same ordering and limits as any activity, so a repeated rejection changes nothing. A rejection that carries no operations cannot repair the surface, so the runtime calls onResyncNeeded with reason stale-action . Building run input yourself buildA2uiForwardedProps is exported from both the root and the headless entry, so a server or a non-React client can produce the same shapes.

records.title: AG-UI delivery
records.summary: Redelivery is normal, so delivery is idempotent AG-UI clients see the same activity more than once. A stream reconnects and replays. A MESSAGES SNAPSHOT restates a whole thread. Two streams carry the same message. AG-UI 1.0 defines no versi
records.text: Redelivery is normal, so delivery is idempotent AG-UI clients see the same activity more than once. A stream reconnects and replays. A MESSAGES SNAPSHOT restates a whole thread. Two streams carry the same message. AG-UI 1.0 defines no version, sequence or idempotency field on activity events, so the runtime cannot rely on the transport to say "you have seen this". Before 4.3.0 every snapshot deleted the surfaces its message had named and replayed that one message. A redelivered activity therefore rolled a surface back and threw away typed input. The runtime now reconciles instead of replays . The rules A surface is deleted only by an explicit deleteSurface . A replace: true snapshot restates what the producer says; it is applied to the held surface as updates. It never deletes a surface and never recreates one. Components the restatement leaves out stay, because the official processor never removes a component the producer stops mentioning. Typed input survives. The runtime remembers the last value the producer wrote at each data leaf and writes only leaves whose producer value changed. An unchanged value cannot overwrite what the user typed. If the producer changes a leaf the user also changed, the producer wins , and onConflict reports it so you can surface it. A leaf the producer wrote earlier and no longer states is removed. A deleted surface stays deleted. A redelivered create or update at or below the version that deleted it cannot revive it. Only versioned deletions are remembered, bounded by maxTombstones . A message absent from a MESSAGES SNAPSHOT leaves its surfaces alone. The snapshot is the complete set of activity messages. A tracked message it omits is forgotten as a message only; its surfaces stay. A snapshot with no activity messages is not handled. Ordering is optional and per surface Because AG-UI has no version field, a producer that wants ordering carries one in the activity's own content: Field Meaning --- --- version An integer that orders one surface's activities. An older version is ignored, an identical one is ignored, a newer one is applied epoch An integer the producer raises on every restart. A restarted producer that numbers from 1 again is not mistaken for an old one. A missing epoch means 0 One activity can touch several surfaces and each is decided on its own. - Same key, different content ( version-conflict ) is a producer fault: the first is kept, the second ignored, and the two are never merged. - A producer that sends no versions is protected only against an identical redelivery of the same message. Out-of-order delivery of versionless activities is not detected, so version your activities if order matters. - Restating createSurface for a held surface applies its inline components and data model as updates. If it changes the catalog, theme or sendDataModel , that surface's operations in the activity are ignored and a surface-config-mismatch fault is reported. Reading what the runtime did Callback Called when --- --- onConflict the producer changed a data leaf the user had also changed onProducerFault a version conflict, a config mismatch, a limit, or a refused batch onResyncNeeded the runtime needs the producer to restate state, see Deltas and resync Upgrading from 4.2.x If you relied on a replace: true restatement to remove a surface or its components, send deleteSurface for the surface you want gone. Components a producer stops mentioning persist in a held surface. This is the one deliberate behavior change in 4.3.0. Only processAgUiEvent tracks and reconciles. Messages passed straight to processMessages are applied as before and are neither versioned nor deduplicated. Each processMessages call is still one transaction: the whole batch is preflighted against a shadow processor, so a later error cannot commit an earlier message.

records.title: Deltas and resync
records.summary: Update a surface without resending it A producer can change a long-lived surface with a small ACTIVITY DELTA instead of a full snapshot. A delta applies on top of the version it names and produces the next one. A deliberately small subset O
records.text: Update a surface without resending it A producer can change a long-lived surface with a small ACTIVITY DELTA instead of a full snapshot. A delta applies on top of the version it names and produces the next one. A deliberately small subset Only two JSON Patch operations are accepted: - add to /a2ui operations/- , which appends an A2UI operation; - test on /surfaceVersions/ /version , and optionally /surfaceVersions/ /epoch . Anything else is rejected with invalid-message . A delta that touches a surface without naming its version is rejected, because it cannot be ordered. remove is rejected because the official processor cannot remove a component. Without an epoch test, the held epoch is assumed. What happens to a delta - In order: applied. The surface moves to the next version. - Already applied or behind: ignored. - Ahead of what is held, or for a surface with no versioned state: held in a bounded buffer ( maxBufferedDeltas , bufferTimeoutMs ). When the missing version arrives, the held deltas apply in order. If it never arrives, or the buffer overflows, the runtime asks for a resync. - A delta touching several surfaces waits as a whole until every surface is in order. Resync onResyncNeeded(request) fires when: request.reason Meaning --- --- gap a delta waited too long for the version it builds on missing-surface a delta named a surface the runtime holds no state for buffer-overflow too many deltas were waiting refused the runtime refused a batch the producer had accepted (a disallowed component, a topology error, a limit) stale-action the server rejected an action as stale and returned nothing to repair it AG-UI has no resync event, so you send the request upstream inside forwardedProps on the next run input: The producer reads forwardedProps.a2uiResync.held , sees exactly which (epoch, version) the client holds per surface, and answers with the operations since then, or a fresh snapshot. dispose() clears the buffer and every pending timer.

records.title: Headless runtime and export
records.summary: Validate on the server exactly as the browser will @prometheus-ags/a2ui-react/headless runs the same validation as the React runtime with no React, no DOM and no renderer. A server mirror, a validator or a compactor can check agent output w
records.text: Validate on the server exactly as the browser will @prometheus-ags/a2ui-react/headless runs the same validation as the React runtime with no React, no DOM and no renderer. A server mirror, a validator or a compactor can check agent output with the identical rules the browser applies. One core, two entries The headless and React runtimes share one core, and both build their catalog with one function from the same default allowlists. The allowlist, the limits, the schema checks, the ordering rules and the all-or-nothing batches are the same code, so they cannot drift apart. Only the catalog's source differs: the headless entry uses the official @a2ui/web core basic catalog, which has no renderers. Nothing it imports reaches @a2ui/react or React at run time. It holds and validates state; it does not render. The headless declaration files still reference shared option types whose default names the React component type, so a type-checking consumer needs @types/react available even though no React code runs. Export a surface exportSurfaceMessages(surfaceId, pruneOrphans? ) is available on both runtimes. It returns surfaceId, messages, orphans : messages that rebuild the surface in a fresh runtime. Exporting the rebuilt surface again yields the same messages. Surface Exported as --- --- v0.9.1 Three official messages: createSurface (catalog, theme, sendDataModel ), updateComponents (every component, with its own catalogId where it differs from the surface's) and updateDataModel at / v1.0 One inline createSurface carrying its components and data model, with each action's wantResponse and responsePath put back where the producer wrote them. The v1.0 schema cannot express a theme, so a v1.0 surface has none to lose An explicit wantResponse: false comes back as an absent field, which means the same thing. Orphans The official processor never removes a component a producer stops mentioning, so unreferenced components accumulate in a long-lived surface. The export treats the component with id root as the anchor and preserves it by id. Components that no reachable component refers to are orphans : they are left out of the export, unless you pass pruneOrphans: false , and listed in orphans so you can see what was dropped. A surface with no root component has nothing to anchor to, so nothing is pruned and orphans is empty. An unknown surface throws a PrometheusA2uiError with code surface-not-found . Typical uses - Server mirror: apply the same AG-UI events on the server to hold authoritative (epoch, version) state, and answer a client's resync request. - Compaction: export a long-lived surface, drop the orphans, and send the result as a fresh snapshot. - Validation: reject an agent's output before it reaches any browser.

records.title: A2UI and AG-UI
records.summary: Agents propose interfaces. Your application keeps the authority. @prometheus-ags/a2ui-react renders interfaces that an agent describes, and it connects that interface to the entity graph without ever giving the agent control of it. This sec
records.text: Agents propose interfaces. Your application keeps the authority. @prometheus-ags/a2ui-react renders interfaces that an agent describes, and it connects that interface to the entity graph without ever giving the agent control of it. This section explains the two protocols involved, what the package guarantees when messages are delivered over AG-UI, and how to wire it up. Two protocols, two jobs Protocol Job What it carries --- --- --- A2UI Describe an interface from a catalog of approved components Surfaces: components, a data model, and the actions a user can take AG-UI Move agent events to the client Runs, messages, tool calls, and activities. An A2UI surface rides inside an activity A2UI is the picture; AG-UI is the delivery truck. They are independent, and the package keeps them apart: the package root is the official A2UI surface, and @prometheus-ags/a2ui-react/ag-ui holds the older AG-UI chat components. What the package guarantees - Validity is not authority. A surface can be perfectly valid A2UI and still be refused. Components come from an allowlist, and every action passes your default-deny policy, with optional human approval. See Limits and security. - Redelivery is safe. Reconnects, thread snapshots and duplicate streams never roll a surface back or erase what the user typed. See AG-UI delivery. - Long-lived surfaces update incrementally. Versioned deltas apply in order, wait when something is missing, and ask for a resync when the gap does not close. See Deltas and resync. - Actions are idempotent. Each interaction carries a globally unique id, so a server can safely handle a retry. See Actions. - Untrusted input is bounded. Resource limits are on by default and reject a whole call rather than truncating it. See Limits and security. - It runs without a browser. A headless entry applies the same validation on a server and can export a surface as messages. See Headless runtime and export. Pick your entry point You want to Import --- --- Render surfaces in React @prometheus-ags/a2ui-react Validate or mirror agent output on a server, or export a surface @prometheus-ags/a2ui-react/headless Keep the pre-3.0 AG-UI chat components @prometheus-ags/a2ui-react/ag-ui Version axes These numbers are related but are not interchangeable: Axis Selected target --- --- Public A2UI input v1.0 release candidate and v0.9.1 Official renderer engine v0.9.1 compatibility boundary @a2ui/react / @a2ui/web core 0.12.0 @a2ui/markdown-it 0.2.0 AG-UI @ag-ui/core peer range =0.0.59 <0.1.0 \ \ ^1.0.0 , developed against 1.0.3 The published A2UI packages do not expose a v1 renderer yet. The runtime validates the v1.0 release-candidate envelope, decomposes its embedded surface into the official v0.9.1 processor, and keeps v1-only action metadata at the boundary. It does not claim an upstream v1 renderer. Quick start The runtime is application-owned. Create it once, pass it to the provider, and call runtime.dispose() when it is no longer needed. Try it The agui-activity-lab example is a real AG-UI producer and a React consumer you can run locally to replay, reorder and overload the runtime and watch what it does. Where the reference lives - Package reference: packages/a2ui-react/README.md - Wire contract and evidence boundary: release/a2ui-protocol-bridge.md - Policy-controlled A2A and A2UI tutorial: Agentic A2UI

records.title: Limits and security
records.summary: Bound what an agent can ask for A2UI messages come from an agent or server your application does not control. Two separate defenses apply, and neither depends on the other. Protocol validity never grants authority Think of the catalog as an
records.text: Bound what an agent can ask for A2UI messages come from an agent or server your application does not control. Two separate defenses apply, and neither depends on the other. Protocol validity never grants authority Think of the catalog as an approved vocabulary, not a database credential. The official processor can prove a surface and an action are valid A2UI. Only your application can decide whether that action may touch a tenant, an entity, or a field. The entity-graph policy therefore fails closed: 1. The action must match the official v0.9.1 schema. 2. The exact action name must be registered. 3. Its context must match your application schema. 4. The entity type, action and every written field must be allowlisted. 5. Your authorize callback must approve scope and tenant access. 6. replace and remove additionally need out-of-band human approval. 7. Only then may the policy call the graph store. Agent-supplied context cannot approve itself. Unknown actions, tenants, entity types and fields are denied. The default catalog also excludes openUrl : navigation is never granted silently. Resource limits The official @a2ui/web core processor enforces no resource caps, so one faulty or hostile producer could exhaust the browser. The runtime enforces limits by default . Nothing is silently truncated. Limit Default Applies to --- --- --- maxSurfaces 64 surfaces held by one runtime maxComponentsPerSurface 2,000 components in one surface maxComponentsTotal 10,000 components across all surfaces maxComponentDepth 32 levels in the longest component reference chain maxDataModelBytes 1,048,576 serialized UTF-8 size of one surface's data model maxComponentBytes 1,048,576 serialized UTF-8 size of one surface's components maxOperationsPerCall 500 messages in one processMessages call maxCallBytes 1,048,576 serialized UTF-8 size of one call maxTrackedMessages 1,000 activity messages remembered for redelivery maxTombstones 1,000 deleted surfaces remembered so a stale create cannot revive them maxBufferedDeltas 100 deltas held while the version they build on is missing bufferTimeoutMs 5,000 how long a held delta waits before a resync is requested The defaults are provisional estimates, not measurements, and are exported as DEFAULT PROMETHEUS A2UI LIMITS . When a limit is exceeded The whole call is rejected before anything is applied, and every surface is left unchanged. onProducerFault receives the limit name, the configured max , the value the call would have produced ( attempted ), the value held before it ( current , for state limits) and the surfaceId for per-surface limits. The call then throws a PrometheusA2uiError with code limit-exceeded . processAgUiEvent goes through processMessages , so it is covered too. maxOperationsPerCall and maxCallBytes are checked on the raw input. The state limits are checked on the state the call would produce, measured on the same shadow processor that preflights the batch, so the numbers are exact. Changing limits at runtime setLimits applies to later calls only and never evicts a surface already held. Calls that grow a value past a lowered cap are rejected, but calls that shrink it or leave it unchanged, such as deleting a surface, still succeed, so the application can get back under the cap. :::warning Upgrading Enforcement is on by default. A host that already renders surfaces larger than these defaults must raise the relevant limits when upgrading, or those calls are rejected with limit-exceeded . ::: Where this fits in the wider security model See Security and tenant boundaries for the graph-level boundaries, and A2A and policy-controlled A2UI for the server side of the same trust model.

records.title: Entity graph theory
records.summary: Why normalized identity changes application behavior When every query owns its own entity copy, a mutation must discover and update every affected cache entry. A normalized graph reverses that responsibility: queries contribute entities and
records.text: Why normalized identity changes application behavior When every query owns its own entity copy, a mutation must discover and update every affected cache entry. A normalized graph reverses that responsibility: queries contribute entities and ordered IDs; readers resolve the current entity at render time. One canonical write therefore updates list rows, detail panels, relationship badges, and agent-generated surfaces together. Local patches overlay canonical data at read time. This allows immediate UI feedback and exact rollback without confusing unsaved state with confirmed server state. Stores and adapters own I/O; hooks and view models orchestrate; components render state and submit intent. This model does not eliminate remote caching, pagination, authorization, or conflict resolution. It gives those concerns one explicit place to interact with entity identity instead of letting framework query containers become the untracked application database.

records.title: Graph lifecycle, SWR, GC, and Suspense
records.summary: From population instruction to collected entity A hook describes an entity or list population instruction and subscribes to the graph. The engine deduplicates concurrent identical work, records subscriber tokens, returns current data, and r
records.text: From population instruction to collected entity A hook describes an entity or list population instruction and subscribes to the graph. The engine deduplicates concurrent identical work, records subscriber tokens, returns current data, and revalidates stale subscribed entries in the background. Focus and reconnect mark subscribed data stale; unsubscribed data is not revalidated merely because it exists. Stale-while-revalidate keeps the last usable projection visible while a service refreshes canonical data. Suspense may coordinate the initial absence of data, but it does not become the state owner. Garbage collection removes entities after the configured retention boundary when no lists, relations, or active subscribers require them. Tune staleTime , retry, and GC from observed application behavior. A shorter timer is not automatically more correct: it increases I/O and can hide an incomplete realtime contract.

records.title: Concepts
records.summary: One identity, many projections The graph separates canonical server-confirmed entities, local-only patches, and ordered list membership. That separation is the mechanism behind cross-view reactivity—not a slogan or a naming convention. Stru
records.text: One identity, many projections The graph separates canonical server-confirmed entities, local-only patches, and ordered list membership. That separation is the mechanism behind cross-view reactivity—not a slogan or a naming convention. Structure Owns Never owns --- --- --- entities[type][id] canonical entity data view-local flags patches[type][id] optimistic and UI augmentation server truth lists[queryKey].ids order, pagination, fetch state copied entities Queries are instructions to populate these structures. They are not durable containers for separate copies of application data. Read the full entity graph theory for data flow, consistency, and trade-offs.

records.title: Realtime, offline, and convergence
records.summary: Realtime is another graph writer Realtime adapters emit ChangeSet objects. RealtimeManager coalesces repeated changes to the same identity within a 16 ms window, producing one store write and one reactive notification. Set the interval to z
records.text: Realtime is another graph writer Realtime adapters emit ChangeSet objects. RealtimeManager coalesces repeated changes to the same identity within a 16 ms window, producing one store write and one reactive notification. Set the interval to zero only when synchronous, unbatched behavior is a measured requirement. Offline persistence stores explicit graph and queue state. PGlite provides a durable local database; Loro providers exchange mergeable operations and use deterministic peer identity. Reconnect first recovers missed state, then drains queued intent. The verified loopback covers delivery order, same-field conflict, echo suppression, snapshot recovery, and forced WebSocket termination. Convergence is not the same as authorization. A valid remote operation still crosses tenant, actor, and policy boundaries before it can mutate the graph.

records.title: SDL and code generation
records.summary: Version the entity contract The SDL describes entity identity, fields, relationships, validation metadata, and generated binding surfaces. Code generation turns that versioned schema into strongly typed models, provider families, transport
records.text: Version the entity contract The SDL describes entity identity, fields, relationships, validation metadata, and generated binding surfaces. Code generation turns that versioned schema into strongly typed models, provider families, transport seams, and relation metadata. Generated files are inspectable artifacts and drift checks fail when the source schema and public declarations disagree. Schema generation does not own runtime data. It defines the contract consumed by stores and adapters; the normalized graph remains the application state authority.

records.title: Views, CRUD, and relationships
records.summary: Local, remote, and hybrid views A transport-agnostic filter can compile to a local predicate, REST parameters, GraphQL variables, or SQL. local mode filters a complete graph without I/O; remote forwards the instruction because local data is
records.text: Local, remote, and hybrid views A transport-agnostic filter can compile to a local predicate, REST parameters, GraphQL variables, or SQL. local mode filters a complete graph without I/O; remote forwards the instruction because local data is incomplete; hybrid projects current local results immediately while a service fetches the remote set. Edit buffers stay outside the graph until save. Explicit optimistic operations write a patch together with the exact previous state needed for rollback. Confirmation replaces canonical data and clears the patch; failure restores the prior projection rather than guessing a compensating value. Relationship schemas make invalidation traversable. When a foreign key changes, the store marks affected lists and related entities stale and follows reverse relations. Realtime sorted insertion uses binary search so a new entity can join a list without sorting copied entity objects.

records.title: AG-UI activity lab
records.summary: See the runtime handle a hostile stream The examples/agui-activity-lab example pairs a real AG-UI 1.0 producer with a React consumer so you can reproduce, by hand or from a test, what a real network does to an agent stream: redelivery, reor
records.text: See the runtime handle a hostile stream The examples/agui-activity-lab example pairs a real AG-UI 1.0 producer with a React consumer so you can reproduce, by hand or from a test, what a real network does to an agent stream: redelivery, reordering, gaps, retries and floods. - The producer is a plain node:http server that streams AG-UI events over Server-Sent Events. Every event is checked against the @ag-ui/core 1.0 schemas first, so the runtime sees a valid AG-UI stream. - The consumer is a Vite and React app. A store owns the connections and the network calls, a hook feeds events to the runtime, and the components only render, following the repository's Components → Hooks → Stores → Services flow. Open http://localhost:5173/?producer=http://127.0.0.1:5176&stream=a,b to follow two streams at once, which reproduces two streams carrying the same activity. Drive the producer with POST /control/emit and read what the consumer sent back from GET /control/envelopes . The example README lists every endpoint. What the acceptance run proves The hardening is verified against this real producer and consumer, not against mocks: 17 browser flows, 4 headless checks and 6 Cucumber scenarios covering redelivery, ordering, deltas, actions, limits and export. Verification is local; see the example README for the commands. Read the concepts first in A2UI and AG-UI.

records.text: Flutter/Riverpod scenario tour The Flutter application projects one graph through generated Riverpod providers, demonstrates optimistic and offline-aware CRUD, relationships, realtime invalidation, policy-gated A2UI 1.0-RC input over GenUI 0.10.2, responsive layouts, and an optional FFI transport. Flutter 3.44.8 generation, analysis, 70 package tests, 25 showcase tests, and three deterministic phone/tablet goldens are recorded. The shared application smoke flow also passed on an Android API 35 emulator and an iOS 26.5 simulator. Physical devices, signing, and app-store delivery remain outside this evidence boundary. A separate assembled debugger flow now launches the configured Flutter app, connects from outside the isolate over Dart VM-service WebSocket JSON-RPC, and exercises two published DevTools controllers through real Riverpod views. It passed with 46 lifecycle, mutation, view, time-travel, and multi-client import events plus redaction, payload-bound, preview-conflict, rewind/live, history-retention, and teardown assertions. The official Flutter DevTools extension build and package layout are validated separately. The reusable library is public as entity graph flutter@3.1.0 . That registry publication is separate from the example's platform evidence.

records.text: Flutter and Riverpod 3 entity graph flutter owns the canonical Dart graph. Generated Riverpod families project entities and lists without copying entity data into widgets. The package covers local/remote/hybrid views, optimistic rollback, realtime invalidation, transports, an optional FFI seam, and cross-view widget goldens. Install the public 3.1.0 package from pub.dev: The published archive passed a clean consumer import and analyzer check. pub.dev does not yet associate the package with a verified publisher, so publisher assignment remains an operational follow-up rather than an installation block. The companion showcase accepts strict A2UI 1.0-RC surface envelopes and normalizes them to GenUI 0.10.2 only after application-owned policy validation. Start with packages/entity graph flutter/README.md and the Flutter example evidence. Optional DevTools Version 3.1.0 includes a separate, optional package:entity graph flutter/devtools.dart library with a reference-counted controller per graph and a store-explicit Dart VM-service bridge. It observes real graph publications and Riverpod logical views, projects canonical/patch/ merged dirty state and relationships, retains bounded history/snapshots, supports conflict-safe preview/restore, and provides rewind/return-live. The controller and official Flutter DevTools companion are included in the published package. Values remain metadata-only unless the host explicitly supplies inclusion and redaction policy. Treat the VM-service URI as a debugger secret and attach only from a host-controlled development mode. The complete controller gate is: It passed through two external VM-service clients on a configured iOS simulator with two isolated graphs and 46 versioned events in the frozen-candidate run. The official Flutter DevTools extension build and package layout are validated separately.

records.title: A2A and policy-controlled A2UI
records.summary: Protocol validity never grants graph authority The A2A package implements the JSON-RPC task lifecycle and caller-scoped task access. A2UI renders official surface messages through a safe widget catalog. An application-owned action catalog v
records.text: Protocol validity never grants graph authority The A2A package implements the JSON-RPC task lifecycle and caller-scoped task access. A2UI renders official surface messages through a safe widget catalog. An application-owned action catalog validates intent, checks policy, requests human approval where required, and only then calls graph/store operations. Malformed messages, unknown widgets, unauthorized actions, cancellation, and denial fail closed. External agents may propose UI or intent; they cannot bypass tenant boundaries, service validation, or the application action policy. Delivering A2UI over AG-UI A2UI surfaces reach the browser as AG-UI activities. The runtime treats that delivery as unreliable: redelivered, restated and out-of-order activities are reconciled instead of replayed, versioned deltas apply in order, every executed action carries a globally unique id, and resource limits bound what an agent can ask for. The full guide is the A2UI and AG-UI section: - AG-UI delivery - Deltas and resync - Actions - Limits and security - Headless runtime and export

records.title: PGlite and Loro
records.summary: Durable local state and peer convergence PGlite persists normalized entities and explicit queue/checkpoint state in a local PostgreSQL-compatible database. Loro adds CRDT convergence as a companion package rather than a core dependency. The
records.text: Durable local state and peer convergence PGlite persists normalized entities and explicit queue/checkpoint state in a local PostgreSQL-compatible database. Loro adds CRDT convergence as a companion package rather than a core dependency. The sync bridge projects provider events into a chosen graph store and suppresses inbound echo. records.title: Tauri native and Flutter FFI
records.summary: Native adapters stay below the store Tauri commands and events provide native persistence and lifecycle seams behind least-privilege capabilities. Flutter's optional FFI transport can call a Rust implementation, but it does not own a second
records.text: Native adapters stay below the store Tauri commands and events provide native persistence and lifecycle seams behind least-privilege capabilities. Flutter's optional FFI transport can call a Rust implementation, but it does not own a second graph. Both paths preserve the language-invariant flow: View → ViewModel → Store → Service → Native boundary. Capability denial, malformed native responses, offline restart, and generated binding drift have explicit tests. Signing, notarization, physical devices, and app-store publication remain release-authority gates.

records.title: REST, GraphQL, WebSocket, and Supabase
records.summary: Transport adapters populate one graph REST adapters normalize response entities and preserve ordered result IDs. GraphQL adapters use the same graph even when selection sets differ; missing fields represent incomplete canonical knowledge, n
records.text: Transport adapters populate one graph REST adapters normalize response entities and preserve ordered result IDs. GraphQL adapters use the same graph even when selection sets differ; missing fields represent incomplete canonical knowledge, not a second query-owned copy. WebSocket and Supabase adapters translate insert/update/delete events into ChangeSet values and let RealtimeManager batch graph writes. Authentication headers, tenant scoping, server validation, and subscription authorization belong in services and adapters. Never embed a service-role key in a browser or generated A2UI surface.

records.title: Migrate from 2.x or an alpha
records.summary: Migrate to the 3.x package family 3.x separates a framework-neutral core from UI bindings, sync, schema, agent, and native packages. The safest migration is a strangler sequence: establish one graph, normalize one entity family, move reader
records.text: Migrate to the 3.x package family 3.x separates a framework-neutral core from UI bindings, sync, schema, agent, and native packages. The safest migration is a strangler sequence: establish one graph, normalize one entity family, move readers, move mutations, then remove the old query-owned copies. 1. Choose one application-owned graph React applications add the core and React binding as one compatible candidate set. Server-rendered applications create a graph per request and hydrate a scoped GraphStoreProvider ; browser-only applications may use the default singleton. Svelte, Solid, Alpine, Web Components, and HTMX resolve the same core peer rather than installing their own runtime graph. 2. Replace copied query data with IDs Before, a mutation commonly rewrote detail and list caches separately: After, one canonical write is sufficient: The list stores next.id ; list and detail readers join the current Task. Both fixtures are compiled by the documentation TypeScript gate. 3. Move I/O below stores Do not migrate a query hook by moving its fetch call into another component hook. Services/adapters own REST, GraphQL, realtime, persistence, and native I/O. Hooks/view models call typed store methods and expose UI state. 4. Separate edit buffers and optimistic patches Keep unsaved form state in the view model. Use a graph patch only for an explicit optimistic experience, record exact previous state, clear the patch on confirmation, and restore the previous projection on failure. 5. Alpha-to-stable moves - Consume the fixed twelve-package stable set; do not mix alpha and 3.x core peers. - Use the official A2UI renderer at the package root; alpha AG-UI chat/state helpers live under the explicit ./ag-ui subpath. - Use the vanilla core store for non-React consumers and scoped server graphs. - Regenerate Riverpod declarations after updating the Dart schema/package. - Re-run packed module, singleton, export-ledger, example, and migration fixtures before removing the old dependency. Keep a rollback commit until the new readers and mutation paths pass their focused consumer tests. Never move latest merely because a source migration compiled.

records.title: Performance and tuning
records.summary: Measure the graph, transport, and projection separately Normalization reduces copied writes, but it does not make every query or render free. Measure entity write frequency, subscriber count, list joins, transport latency, persistence time,
records.text: Measure the graph, transport, and projection separately Normalization reduces copied writes, but it does not make every query or render free. Measure entity write frequency, subscriber count, list joins, transport latency, persistence time, and bundle payload independently. - Keep lists as IDs so a canonical change does not rebuild copied rows. - Let RealtimeManager coalesce bursty updates; change its 16 ms interval only from observed latency or render evidence. - Use local view mode only when completeness is proven. Hybrid mode can provide immediate local results while remote data reconciles. - Tune stale and GC times to real navigation/reconnect behavior. Aggressive revalidation can hide a broken subscription while increasing I/O. - Keep CRDT, A2A, A2UI, Tauri, and UI packages optional so consumers pay only for selected capabilities. - Compare bundle sizes with the same minification, tree-shaking, compression, and peer-dependency methodology. Lighthouse delivery budgets are mobile performance ≥90, accessibility/best practices/SEO ≥95, LCP ≤2.5 s, and CLS ≤0.1. They are T3 deployment gates, not the edit loop.

records.title: Security and tenant boundaries
records.summary: Name the authority at every external boundary The graph is application state, not an authorization system. A client-visible entity never proves that the current actor may read, mutate, subscribe to, or publish it. Enforce authorization in t
records.text: Name the authority at every external boundary The graph is application state, not an authorization system. A client-visible entity never proves that the current actor may read, mutate, subscribe to, or publish it. Enforce authorization in the service and persistence boundaries that own those operations. Tenant and transport rules - Derive tenant scope from a validated identity claim; do not accept a client tenant ID as authority. - Apply row-level security and service validation independently of client filters. A local FilterSpec is presentation, not access control. - Scope realtime subscriptions by tenant, channel, and consumer. Persist checkpoints with that identity so offsets cannot cross tenants. - Validate issuer, audience, expiry, algorithm, kid , JWKS source, and role at the Flint/Gate boundary. Keep signing, verification, and service-role keys separate. - Never expose Forge provisioning or Supabase service-role credentials in web, Flutter, Tauri frontend, documentation, screenshots, or agent prompts. Agent and generated UI rules A2A protocol validity and A2UI schema validity do not grant graph authority. Render only an allowlisted widget catalog. Map actions through an application-owned catalog with argument validation, tenant/actor policy, and human approval where the action has consequential effects. Unknown, malformed, cancelled, or denied actions fail before store mutation. The A2UI runtime also bounds untrusted agent output with resource limits that are enforced by default, and it mints every action id itself rather than trusting one from the agent. See Limits and security. Native rules Tauri capabilities grant the minimum command/event surface. Validate every native response before projection. Flutter FFI is a transport seam, not a way to hide a second graph or bypass Dart-side policy. Signing, notarization, and store distribution are independent release authorities. Development tooling and debugger rules DevTools are local debugging capabilities, not application authorization or a production administration API. Keep ordinary application entries independent of optional tooling entries, activate tooling only under an explicit host-owned development condition, and remove it from production artifacts. For Flutter, package:entity graph flutter/devtools.dart registers store- explicit methods and events through the Dart VM service only when service extensions are available. Treat the VM-service URI and its authentication token as secrets. Do not proxy it onto an untrusted network, record it in evidence, or expose it from an application endpoint. Every graph uses an explicit store ID; there is no implicit default graph across the isolate. Flutter DevTools values are metadata-only by default. A host may enable values only with an application-owned policy and required redactor. Commands cannot escalate that policy, replace the redactor, or commit a preview. Requests, responses, events, history, and snapshots retain simultaneous byte/count ceilings. Detach every retained binding so a disposed application graph is removed from debugger discovery. The controller, bridge, and official Flutter DevTools extension are published in pub.dev 3.1.0 . The assembled acceptance proves the real VM-service and Riverpod boundary; official extension build validation is recorded separately. Secret and evidence handling Release workflows use GitHub OIDC and stage-only npm authority. NPM TOKEN and NODE AUTH TOKEN are prohibited in the RC stage. Documentation text is scanned for token-shaped strings and internal absolute paths. Image publication is fail-closed on exact source and receipt hashes, exact successful receipt values, minimum dimensions, nonblank entropy, and a hash-bound human review for visible secrets and internal paths. Published originals are re-encoded to remove source metadata; only allowlisted assets enter the gallery. Flutter/Xcode child processes must also remove inherited CARGO REGISTRY TOKEN , NPM TOKEN , and NODE AUTH TOKEN before diagnostic capture. Acceptance receipts retain bounded structured assertions and hashes, never raw tool output, VM-service URIs, debugger tokens, entity values, or host-local absolute paths.

records.title: Entity management skills
records.summary: Skills are guidance bound to public ledgers The prometheus-entity-skills tree helps agents detect a domain, initialize or migrate a graph, build CRUD and relationship flows, configure GraphQL/Prisma and realtime, add local-first behavior, a
records.text: Skills are guidance bound to public ledgers The prometheus-entity-skills tree helps agents detect a domain, initialize or migrate a graph, build CRUD and relationship flows, configure GraphQL/Prisma and realtime, add local-first behavior, and audit GC/performance. Shared references record architecture rules and runtime export ledgers. Before following a skill, read its complete SKILL.md and required references. After a public API change, run pnpm run refresh:exports only when the export surface actually changed, then pnpm run verify:skills . Package-specific ledgers must match packed/public artifacts; a snippet that only works through a local source alias is not public guidance. Skills never override the core architecture: components/views render, hooks or view models orchestrate, stores own state, and services/adapters own I/O. They also cannot promote themselves based on their own review; adversarial review and human approval gate rule or skill promotion.

records.title: Testing and troubleshooting
records.summary: Test the narrowest truthful boundary During implementation, run the touched TypeScript check and targeted unit. At a completed documentation phase, run content/schema checks, snippet compilation, generated parity, a full Docusaurus build, l
records.text: Test the narrowest truthful boundary During implementation, run the touched TypeScript check and targeted unit. At a completed documentation phase, run content/schema checks, snippet compilation, generated parity, a full Docusaurus build, link/search/sitemap validation, and representative desktop/mobile routes. Browser visual, Lighthouse, device, and deployed-route suites are delivery gates. Common failures A list does not update after an entity mutation Confirm that the list stores the entity ID and the view resolves rows through the same graph. Look for copied response objects or a binding that resolved a second core version. A hook loops or refetches continuously Check stable option/callback identities, the list's lastFetched and stale state, subscriber registration, and whether a terminal service error was recorded. Do not add retries without naming the observed failure scenario. Next.js users see each other's state Remove the mutable server singleton. Create a graph per request, serialize its state, and hydrate a scoped client provider. Realtime begins on the client. Realtime reconnect duplicates or loses state Inspect tenant/channel/consumer identity, the last acknowledged checkpoint, offset resume, snapshot recovery, and echo suppression. A green loopback test does not prove live credentials or hosted infrastructure. npm staging returns E401/E403 Run npm login --auth-type=web , confirm the account has write access and 2FA, then run pnpm run release:npm-trust:verify . The exact trust must name Prometheus-AGS/prometheus-entity-management , publish.yml , npm-rc , and only stage-publish permission. Do not add a long-lived token to make OIDC pass. GitHub Pages loads the homepage but deep routes fail Verify baseUrl , explicit trailing slashes, .nojekyll , and that every route probe uses /prometheus-entity-management/ . Search assets and evidence URLs must also resolve below the repository base path.

The Pages deployment does not rebuild native documentation or install native toolchains. It runs pnpm run docs:native-api:check , which hashes every declared native source and every committed dartdoc/rustdoc artifact and compares them with the checked-in manifest. Any source, file, byte, or inventory drift fails before deployment; full regeneration remains the stronger release gate. The curated Flutter guides link provider families, graph operations, views, transports, and the optional FFI seam to this dartdoc surface.
